newsitem.title: CHINA: China shares indices close generally higher.
newsitem.headline: China shares indices close generally higher.

text.p: China's A and B shares indices ended mostly higher in active trading on Tuesday despite new rules banning securities rule violators from holding senior positions in the industry or from trading, brokers said.
Shanghai's B index inched up 0.362 points or 0.53 percent to 68.491 points on volume of 29.3 million shares worth US$13.0 million.

The rules, issued by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), said company officials found to engage in insider trading and traders found to manipulate prices would be banned from the industry permanently or for several years.
Brokers said that active buying supported the market despite the news, with market sentiment good.

In China's fledgling and highly speculative markets, news of tighter regulation is normally greeted with by across-the-board falls. However, analysts said the gains on Tuesday indicate investors have confidence in the long-term outlook and stable development of the market.
"We are seeing fresh capital flowing into the market, which improved market sentiment," one broker said.
Another broker said there was more buying than profit-taking at current levels because most investors view B shares as being undervalued compared to their A share equivalents.
"The index will breach the current level soon given the strong market sentiment," he said.
Huangshan Tourism was the star after a recent period of consolidation, rising $0.028 or 6.19 percent to $0.480 on volume of 4.6 million shares.
Clothing maker Shanghai Kaikai was the most traded counter and became the second-biggest winner on institutional buying, gaining $0.014 or 3.95 percent to $0.368 on volume of 4.6 million shares.
Shanghai A shares reversed early losses caused by the new rules due to an inflow of speculative money, brokers said.
The index rose 5.336 points or 0.48 percent to 1,116.792 points on volume of 840.5 million shares worth 8.3 billion yuan.
The SSE30 index edged up 1.871 points or 0.07 percent to 2,874.359 points.
Shanghai Fello was the star on institutional buying, soaring 0.88 yuan or 10.03 percent to 9.65 yuan on volume of 20.5 million shares.
Shenzhen's B share index closed lower due to the new rules, brokers said.
The B share index slipped 0.63 points or 0.41 percent to 155.00 on turnover of HK$74.45 million, down from Monday's HK$108.26 million.
"The regulations aimed at reducing speculation dampened sentiment," said an analyst with a major Chinese brokerage.
Shenzhen and Shanghai stock exchanges last Friday also ordered all brokerages to make public each day's five most-active stocks and the major traders.

"The market will digest the news before too long," said another analyst. "The index will not fall sharply unless there is other bad news, because investors are generally optimistic about China's 1997 economic outlook.
The A share index reversed early losses to close up 2.05 points or 0.52 percent at 400.27. Turnover was 10.81 billion yuan against 11.12 billion yuan on Monday.
Brokers said they expected the A share index to rise further this week.
"Investors' confidence remains strong despite Beijing's crackdown, especially for listed companies expected to post better 1996 results," said an analyst with China Securities.
On the Shenzhen's B share market, China Southern Glass was the biggest loser, down HK$0.15 or 2.96 percent to HK$4.92 on volume of 982,400 shares.
Power supplier Zhuhai Huadian performed strongest on the A share market, surging 0.62 yuan or 10 percent to end limit-up at 6.82 yuan with 6.82 million shares changing hands.
